_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-01.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed.

Then every kept place that marks three or more poetry lines as said twice, opposite, building or climbing was read again by two readers, a third settling any difference: each kept all its lines, kept only the lines that stand in the relation, or was dropped ("span").

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Then every kept place marked as said twice was read again by two readers, a third settling any difference: each kept, moved to the form its lines plainly show (a judge's form only where a reader proposed it), or dropped ("label").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.

Strong's tags are also taken off any kept place whose tags light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, or whose roots light more words of the verse than there are tags, or, on a question or parallel lines, that were chosen for marked words since changed: such tags are a stretch of words, or name words no longer marked.

places.why: "If Cain is avenged sevenfold, / then Lamech seventy-sevenfold" does not say the first line again. The two lines are built the same way (a name and a number), and the second completes the first, so it is building, not same.

The BSB plainly turns the words around: sheds, blood, man / man, blood, shed. The man who sheds blood becomes the one whose blood is shed. That is not a restatement. Lines 3-4 give the reason, so they are left out of the words.

Lines 1-2 (peoples serve / nations bow down) and lines 3-4 (master of your brothers / sons of your mother bow down) each say the same thing twice. Lines 5-6 (curse / bless) set opposites against each other, so the words stop at line 4.
places.span_why: "May peoples serve you / and nations bow down to you" is one pair, and "master of your brothers / sons of your mother bow down" is a second pair about other people, not a restatement of the nations. Keep the clearest pair.
places.label: all

places.why: "Who can count the dust of Jacob / or number even a fourth of Israel?" and "Let me die the death of the righteous; / let my end be like theirs!" are two plain restating pairs, and they show in the BSB itself. The tags include the object marker H0853, leave out "count" and "dust", and skip the second pair.
places.span_why: "Who can count the dust of Jacob / or number even a fourth of Israel?" restate each other, but "Let me die the death of the righteous" begins a separate pair on a different subject.
places.label: all

places.why: "He considers no disaster for Jacob; / He sees no trouble for Israel" and "The LORD their God is with them, / and the shout of the King is among them" plainly restate each other in the BSB. The tags cover "not", Jacob and line 2, but miss line 1's "looked" and "disaster" and all of lines 3-4.
places.span_why: "He considers no disaster for Jacob; / He sees no trouble for Israel" is a plain restatement. "The LORD their God is with them" is a second pair with a new thought.
places.label: all

places.why: "no spell against Jacob / and no divination against Israel" is plainly said twice. Lines 3-4 are one sentence, where line 4 is what will be said, so the words stop at line 2. The tags take in "this time" and "it will be said", and miss "enchantment".
places.label: all

places.why: "How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, / your dwellings, O Israel!" plainly says the first line again, and the BSB shows it. The tags mark "dwellings" but not "tents", so half of the pair is missing.
places.label: all

places.why: "He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob / and Your law to Israel" and "he will set incense before You / and whole burnt offerings on Your altar" are parallel pairs: the verb is carried over and the second line names the same service in other words. The tags mark "law" but not its pair "ordinances", and lines 3-4 have no tags.
places.span_why: "teach Your ordinances to Jacob / and Your law to Israel" restate each other, but "set incense before You / and whole burnt offerings" is a separate pair about another duty.
places.label: all

places.why: "So Israel dwells securely; / the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled" is plainly said twice (Israel / fountain of Jacob, securely / untroubled). Lines 3-4 add the setting and do not restate. The tags (Israel, security, alone, spring, Jacob) are the paired words of lines 1-2.
places.label: all

places.why: "I will sing to the LORD; / I will sing praise to the LORD" plainly says the first line again. Line 1 is a pair inside a single line and does not restate line 2, and line 4 only completes line 3. The one tag, H0238 "give ear", is not on these lines.
places.label: all

places.why: "They were swifter than eagles, / they were stronger than lions" is a plain parallel pair praising their might, with "they were" repeated. Lines 1-2 make up one sentence that line 2 completes, so they are left out.
places.label: form
places.label_why: "They were swifter than eagles, / they were stronger than lions": the second line gives a second, different quality (strength after speed), so it builds on the first rather than saying it again.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "May the day of my birth perish, / and the night it was said, / 'A boy is conceived.'" The later lines do not say the first again. They add a second, different time to the curse: the night of conception as well as the day of birth. Verses 4 to 10 then curse each one in turn ("that day" in 3:4, "that night" from 3:6), so the lines build on the first.

places.span_why: "turned to darkness" and "may no light shine upon it" plainly say the same thing. "May God above disregard it" adds a new thought about God.
places.label: all

places.span_why: "May it not appear among the days of the year; / may it never be entered in any of the months" restate each other. "If only darkness had taken that night away!" is a different picture.
places.label: all

places.why: "There the wicked cease from raging, / and there the weary find rest": the lines are built the same way ("there the X..."), but line 2 names a different group, the weary instead of the wicked. It adds the other side rather than saying line 1 again, so it is building, not same.

"It stood still, / but I could not discern its appearance; / a form loomed before my eyes, / and I heard a whispering voice" tells a vision step by step. The "but" does not set opposite lines against each other, and the lines are not built alike, so no parallel form plainly shows.

"Call out if you please, but who will answer? / To which of the holy ones will you turn?": line 2 asks line 1's question again in other words. The "but" sits inside line 1, and nothing is set opposite between the lines.
places.label: all

places.why: "For He wounds, but He also binds; / He strikes, but His hands also heal": the opposites are inside each line, and line 2 says line 1 again (wounds / strikes, binds / heal). Between the lines it is said twice.
places.label: all

places.why: "For now you are of no help; / you see terror, and you are afraid": line 2 gives the reason and does not restate line 1. The lines are not built alike either, so neither same nor building plainly shows.

"The eye that beholds me will no longer see me. / You will look for me, but I will be no more": line 2 says line 1 again (no longer see me / I will be no more). The "but" is inside line 2, and nothing is set opposite between the lines.
places.label: all

places.why: "As a cloud vanishes and is gone, / so he who goes down to Sheol does not come back up" is an as/so likeness: line 1 is the picture and line 2 is what it is compared to. It is not a restatement, and the likeness already has its own place (job-7-9-simile-seen).

"I loathe my life! I would not live forever. / Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath" moves from a complaint to a plea with its reason. It does not restate line 1, and the lines are not built alike. The metaphor "my days are but a breath" already has its own place (job-7-16-metaphor-seen).

"Why do You not pardon my transgression / and take away my iniquity?" plainly restates (pardon / take away, transgression / iniquity). Lines 3-4 go on to his death, and their "but" is inside line 4, so no lines are set opposite. The words stop at line 2.
places.label: all

places.why: "He leans on his web, but it gives way; / he holds fast, but it does not endure": line 2 says line 1 again (leans / holds fast, gives way / does not endure). The "but" is inside each line, not set between them.
places.label: all

places.why: "Yes, I know that it is so, / but how can a mortal be righteous before God?" grants a point and then asks a question. Line 2 is not the opposite of line 1. The question that is not asking already has its own place (job-9-2-question-seen).

"If I summoned Him and He answered me, / I do not believe He would listen to my voice." is one conditional sentence: the second line is the outcome of the first, not a restatement, and the two lines are not built alike, so no parallel form fits plainly. The tag on "gave ear to" (H0238) marks an ordinary verb that carries no figure.

"He does not let me catch my breath, / but overwhelms me with bitterness." Both lines describe God afflicting Job, so the "but" does not set an opposite sense. The lines are built alike (He does not let me... / [He] overwhelms me...), and the second adds what He does instead of giving rest. That is plainly lines that build. "Said twice" is less certain, because bitterness is a new element and not the first line in other words.

"If it is a matter of strength, / He is indeed mighty! / If it is a matter of justice, / who can summon Him?" Lines 1 and 3 share the same opening words and lines 2 and 4 give the answers, so the pattern is plainly A B A' B'. Strength and justice are different matters, so the second pair does not restate the first, and "said twice" is the wrong form.

"I would still dread all my sufferings; / I know that You will not acquit me." The second line gives a new thought, the reason for the dread, so it does not restate the first. The two lines are built alike (I would still dread... / I know that...), and the second plainly adds to the first, which is lines that build.

"I will express my complaint / and speak in the bitterness of my soul." plainly say one thing twice: speaking out his grief. Line 1, "I loathe my own life;", is a different statement that leads into them, so the marked words are narrowed to lines 2 and 3.
places.label: all

places.why: "If only I had never come to be, / but had been carried from the womb to the grave." Both lines make one wish, never to have lived, and 10:18 just before makes the same wish. The "but" does not set up an opposite sense. The second line plainly restates the first in other words.
places.label: form
places.label_why: "If only I had never come to be, / but had been carried from the womb to the grave." The second line goes on with the wish and says how it would have happened, so it completes the first line rather than saying it again.

places.why: "You will call, and I will answer; / You will desire the work of Your hands." The second line adds God's longing for His creature as a new thought and does not restate the call and answer. Both lines are built alike ("You will..."), and the second adds to the first: lines that build.

"If his sons receive honor, he does not know it; / if they are brought low, he is unaware." The two lines are built exactly alike, and the second adds the opposite case with the same result. It does not restate the first line's condition, so "said twice" is not plain, and the lines are not opposed in sense. Lines that build fits plainly.

"He despairs of his return from darkness; / he is marked for the sword." The second line brings in a new fate, a violent death, so it does not restate his despair. The lines are built alike (He despairs... / he is marked...), and the second adds to the first: lines that build.

"He wanders about as food for vultures; / he knows the day of darkness is at hand." These are two different thoughts, his wandering and his knowledge that doom is near, so the second does not restate the first. Both lines are built alike (He wanders... / he knows...), and the second adds to the first: lines that build.

"I could also speak like you / if you were in my place; / I could heap up words against you / and shake my head at you." The second pair is built like the first ("I could...") and spells it out further, adding heaped words and a shaken head. That is lines that build, not a plain restatement.

"They open their mouths against me / and strike my cheeks with contempt; / they join together against me." Each line names a different hostile act in the same build (they do this... against me), adding to the one before. That is plainly lines that build, not lines that say the same thing twice.

The only contrast, "I was at ease, but He shattered me;", is inside line 1, not between lines. Line 2, "He seized me by the neck and crushed me.", carries on the shattering and does not oppose it. Line 3, "He has set me up as His target;", begins the archery picture that runs into 16:13. The marked lines do not plainly stand in any one parallel relation.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "He breaks me with wound upon wound; / He rushes me like a mighty warrior." "Breaks" and "rushes" are not words that match: the second line adds another act, the warrior's charge, so it builds on the first rather than saying it again.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "I have sewn sackcloth over my skin; / I have buried my horn in the dust." The second line names a second, different act of mourning. It does not restate the first.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; / the grave awaits me." The second line adds where this ends, the grave, which follows from the first line.

places.why: "My days have passed; my plans are broken off— / even the desires of my heart." The second line is not a clause of its own. It is an appositive that finishes line 1 by naming what the plans are. It is not built like the first line, so Bullinger's "similar form of construction" does not hold, and as a whole line it does not restate "My days have passed." No parallel form fits plainly.

"His vigorous stride is shortened, / and his own schemes trip him up." The second line adds a new thought, that his own schemes cause his fall, so it is not plainly the first said again. Both lines are built alike (his stride... / his own schemes...), and the second adds to the first: lines that build.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "He tears me down on every side until I am gone; / He uproots my hope like a tree." The second line moves to a different thing, "my hope" and not "me", with a new picture of a tree, so it adds to the first rather than restating it.

places.why: The "but" falls inside line 1, so the lines are not opposites. Line 2, "though I implore him with my own mouth", takes "I call for my servant" a step further, from calling to begging, so it builds on line 1.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "The righteous see it and are glad" is followed by a further, outward act, "the innocent mock them:", and that line opens the mocking words of 22:20. Mocking adds to the gladness instead of saying it again.

places.span_why: "the command of His lips" and "the words of His mouth" restate each other. "more than my daily bread" finishes the sentence with a new comparison and restates nothing.
places.label: all

places.why: Hunger is not the opposite of nakedness. "Without clothing, they wander about naked" and "They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry" name two hardships side by side: line 2 adds hunger to nakedness.
"They crush olives within their walls; they tread the winepresses" is built the same way, but line 2 adds a new point, "but go thirsty". It builds on line 1 rather than only saying it again.

"As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned" is an as/so likeness, picture then meaning, not a restatement. The likeness already has its own place (job-24-19-simile-seen).

Line 4, "So injustice is like a broken tree", is a closing likeness with its own place (job-24-20-simile-seen), and "the worm feeds on them" does not restate "The womb forgets them". Lines 1 to 3 are short lines that each add to the picture of their end, so they are marked as building.
"His eyes are on their ways" is not plainly the opposite of "a sense of security". It reads as a threat only if the reader infers judgment, so the opposition is in doubt.

"They are exalted for a moment" is set against "then they are gone", so the four lines do not all say one thing. Lines 3 and 4 plainly do restate each other: "brought low and gathered up" and "cut off like heads of grain". The marked words are narrowed to those two lines.
places.label: all
form
places.label_why: "I will never say that you are right; / I will maintain my integrity until I die": the second line does not say the first again. It adds a further resolve, to keep his integrity for life.

places.why: The reversal is already inside line 1 ("He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more"). Line 2, "when he opens his eyes, all is gone", pairs waking with lying down and completes the loss rather than opposing line 1.
Both lines start with "when", but "when the friendship of God rested on my tent" does not say "when I was in my prime" again. It adds what made those days good, so it builds on line 1.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "I was a father to the needy, / and I took up the case of the stranger" adds a second, different deed for a different group, like the list in 29:15, rather than saying the first again.

places.why: "They abhor me and keep far from me; they do not hesitate to spit in my face": the two lines are built alike, and line 2 is a worse act, not a restatement. It goes beyond line 1.

"They tear up my path; they profit from my destruction, with no one to restrain them": each line adds something new (the tearing up, their profit, no one restraining them), so the lines build. They do not say one thing twice.

The "but" is inside line 1. "When I stand up, You merely look at me" says again what "I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer" says: Job appeals and God does not help. That is said twice, not opposite.
places.label: all

places.why: The "but" is inside line 1 ("blackened, but not by the sun"). Line 2, "I stand up in the assembly and cry for help", is built like line 1 ("I go about" and "I stand up") and adds a second misery. Nothing in it is opposite to line 1.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "My skin grows black and peels" is followed by a different affliction in a different part of the body, "and my bones burn with fever." The second line adds a new suffering instead of restating the first.

places.why: "If my steps have turned from the path, / if my heart has followed my eyes, / or if impurity has stuck to my hands" lists three different ways of sinning (steps, desire, hands). No line plainly says another again.

"Oh, that I had one to hear me!" and "Here is my signature" do not restate the later lines. "Let the Almighty answer me; let my accuser compose an indictment" restates only if the accuser is God, which the verse does not make plain. These two lines are plainly built alike ("Let ... let ..."), so they are kept as building.
"I would give account of all my steps; I would approach Him like a prince": the lines are built alike, but line 2 adds how he would come before God. It does not say line 1 again.

"I waited while you spoke; I listened to your reasoning" plainly says the same thing twice. Line 3, "as you searched for words," is a time clause running on into 32:12, so it is left out. The pairing is plain in the BSB, and the lone tag on "I gave ear" does not carry a figure that spans two lines.
places.label: all

places.why: "hear my speech, and listen to all my words" plainly restates itself in the BSB. The single tag on "give ear" (and not on its partner "hear") does not carry a figure that lies in the two lines.
places.label: all

places.why: "He puts my feet in the stocks; He watches over all my paths": the word pair feet/paths and the two hostile acts say one thing twice. God hems in Job's going, and 33:10 ("He counts me as His enemy") sets the hostile sense.
places.label: form
places.label_why: "He puts my feet in the stocks" is followed by a different act, "He watches over all my paths." Being held fast and being watched are two separate acts of a jailer, so the second line adds to the first.

places.why: "Hear my words, O wise men; give ear to me, O men of learning" plainly restates itself in the BSB (hear/give ear, wise men/men of learning). A lone tag on "give ear" does not carry the two-line figure.
places.label: all

places.why: "hear this; listen to my words" plainly restates the call to listen in the BSB. The single tag on "give ear" does not carry a figure that spans the two lines.
places.label: all

places.why: "The people convulse and pass away; the mighty are removed without human hand" plainly restates itself. Lines 1 and 2 are one clause ("They die in an instant, in the middle of the night") and do not restate each other, so they are left out.
places.label: all

places.why: "Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man": the second line drops the verb and applies the same claim to righteousness, which completes the thought. So it is built on, not a restatement.

The "but" is inside line 1 ("they cry out, but He does not answer"). Line 2, "because of the pride of evil men," only gives the reason as the sentence runs on. No opposite is set against line 1, and no other parallel is plain.

"I get my knowledge from afar, and I will ascribe justice to my Maker": the second line says something new and does not restate the first. The two statements are not plainly parallel enough to mark as built on either.

The "but" is inside line 1. Line 2, "He is mighty in strength of understanding," takes up "mighty" and adds to it rather than opposing line 1. The interrupting "despises no one" keeps it from plainly climbing, so no live form is plain.

"He does not take His eyes off the righteous, but He enthrones them with kings and exalts them forever": every line favours the righteous, so nothing is opposed. The lines run on as one sentence, with no other plain parallel.

"Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God": both lines call Job to attend, and the second adds standing still and names what "this" is. So it builds on the first, which is plain in the BSB. The lone tag on "listen" does not carry the figure.
"You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop": the "but" is inside line 1, and line 2 restates the same limit in other words. It is said twice, not opposite.
places.label: all
form
places.label_why: "Will the wild ox consent to serve you? / Will he stay by your manger at night?" The second line adds a different act, staying by the manger at night, and does not repeat "serve".

places.why: "The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully, but cannot match the pinions and feathers of the stork": line 2 shares line 1's subject and qualifies it within one sentence. It is not a parallel line of opposite sense, and no other parallel is plain.

"He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he charges into battle": the second line is the next action in a sequence and does not restate the first. There is no plain parallel form to mark as built on either.

"I have spoken once, but I have no answer" / "twice, but I have nothing to add": each "but" is inside its own line. Line 2 restates line 1 ("no answer" / "nothing to add"), so it is said twice, not opposite.
places.label: all

places.why: "Who can strip off his outer coat? Who can approach him with a bridle?": two plainly parallel "Who can" questions. The second names a different challenge, his mouth after his coat, so it builds on the first rather than restating it.

"His snorting flashes with light, and his eyes are like the rays of dawn": both lines describe light shining from him. The second adds a different feature, his eyes, so it builds on the first rather than restating it.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, / and on His law he meditates day and night." The second line adds another act, meditating day and night, to the delight of the first.

places.why: "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me." The second line does not restate the first. It goes on to waking and gives the reason, so the couplet plainly builds.
The two questions make different charges (honor maligned; loving vanity and lies), so "same" is not plain. Both lines plainly open with "How long". "Selah" is left out.

"Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning." plainly makes the same plea twice. It shows in the BSB lines, not only in the original, and the one tag on H0238 does not carry a two-line parallel.
places.label: all

places.why: "Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit." pairs throats with tongues and says the same of their speech. Lines 1 and 2 are a separate pair (mouth, then inward part) and do not restate lines 3 and 4, so only lines 3 and 4 are marked.
places.label: form
places.label_why: "Their throats are open graves; / their tongues practice deceit." The organs match, but the second line names a second failing, deceit, beside the deadly speech of the first.

places.why: "if I have rewarded my ally with evil, if I have plundered my foe without cause" adds a second case against a different person (ally, then foe). It does not restate the first, so it builds.

"Put an end to the evil of the wicked, but establish the righteous" plainly sets opposites (end and establish, wicked and righteous). "O righteous God who searches hearts and minds" only addresses God, so it is left out.
"He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making." The second line gives what came of the digging. It builds and does not restate.
"You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor." The second line adds the crowning, so it builds rather than restates.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart; / I will recount all Your wonders." The second line adds a further act, telling His wonders, after the thanks.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "I will be glad and rejoice in You; / I will sing praise to Your name, O Most High." The second line adds a new act, singing praise, to the gladness of the first.

places.span_why: "You have rebuked the nations; / You have destroyed the wicked" restate each other, with the nations and the wicked as the same people. "You have erased their name forever and ever" goes a step further, so it is not a plain restatement.
places.label: all

places.why: "The enemy has come to eternal ruin, / and You have uprooted their cities; / the very memory of them has vanished" gives three different pictures (ruin, cities uprooted, memory gone). No two lines plainly say the same thing again in other words.

"The LORD is known by the justice He brings; the wicked are ensnared by the work of their hands." The second line has a new subject and shows how that justice works, so it builds. "Higgaion Selah" is no part of it and is left out.

places.span_why: "He lies in wait" and "he lurks" plainly say the same thing. "he catches the lowly in his net" moves on from waiting to the catch itself and brings in a new picture, the net.
places.label: all

places.why: "The LORD is King forever and ever; the nations perish from His land." The second line tells what follows from His reign, with a new subject. It builds and does not restate.

"You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts." The second line adds the strengthening, so it builds. "You will incline Your ear," runs on into 10:18 and is left out.

"The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne." plainly restates. "His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men" is a second pair that says something different, so it does not belong in this place. It would need a place of its own.
places.label: all

places.why: The lines do not restate one another: one question runs over lines 1 and 2, and line 3 is about the enemy. What plainly shows is the two questions both opening with "How long". Only the lines that open that way are marked.

No line restates another. After the question, "They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon the LORD." is a couplet whose second line adds a further charge, so it builds. The question line is not part of that couplet and is left out.

The three lines (a wish, "When the LORD restores...", "let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!") do not restate one another. The only pair that does sits inside one BSB line, so it cannot be marked as lines. The tags fall on unrelated words and skip H8055 "be glad", and the figure is not only in the original.

"You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand." plainly restates (joy and pleasures, presence and right hand). "You have made known to me the path of life" is a different thought and is left out.
places.label: all

places.why: "Hear, O LORD, my righteous plea; listen to my cry. Give ear to my prayer" makes the same plea three times. "it comes from lips free of deceit" describes the prayer instead and is left out. The one tag on H0238 does not carry the parallel, and the figure shows in the BSB, not only in the original.
places.label: all

places.why: The marks take "You have tried my heart" and "You have tested me and found no evil" but skip the line between them, "You have visited me in the night", and the later line adds a result ("found no evil"). That is not the verse's own grouping, so in doubt it does not go live.
places.span_why: "You have tried my heart" and "You have tested me" plainly restate each other. "You have visited me in the night" does not plainly mean testing to a reader of the English.
places.label: drop

places.why: "The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded" plainly restates (the LORD and the Most High, thundered and resounded). "hailstones and coals of fire" repeats a phrase from 18:12, does not restate them, and is left out.
places.label: all

places.why: "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters." The second line tells the next step of the rescue and where it was from. It plainly builds, while "same" is doubtful.
"He rescued me because He delighted in me" adds the reason to "He brought me out into the open". It does not just say the first line again, so the form is Built on, not Said twice.

Shield, upholding right hand and exalting gentleness are three different acts, and "exalts me" goes further than protection. Each line adds to the one before, so the lines are Built on rather than Said twice.
"I did not turn back until they were consumed" carries the chase in line 1 on to its end. The second line adds to the first, so this is Built on.
Arming him for battle and then subduing his foes are two steps, and the second is the result of the first. The second line adds to the first, so this is Built on.

Each "but" falls inside its own line, so nothing is set against an opposite. The second line, "to the LORD, but He did not answer", has no verb of its own and completes the first, adding the new point that they cried even to the LORD. That makes it Built on.

The verse moves from rescue ("delivered me from the strife") to rule ("head of nations", "a people ... shall serve me"). The later lines add to the first rather than restating it, so this is Built on.

places.span_why: "delivers me from my enemies" and "rescue me from violent men" plainly restate each other. "You exalt me above my foes" is a different act, lifting up rather than rescuing.

places.why: The BSB's four lines alternate. "I cry out by day" pairs with "and by night", and "but You do not answer" pairs with "but I have no rest": A B A' B'. Nothing is opposed in sense.

places.why: "He guides me in the paths of righteousness" is a new act, not "He restores my soul" said again, and "for the sake of His name" completes it. The lines are Built on.
places.span_why: "He restores my soul; / He guides me in the paths of righteousness" are built alike, each adding a second act of the Shepherd. "for the sake of His name" only gives the reason for His guiding, which the rules do not count.

places.why: "The LORD preserves the faithful, but fully repays the arrogant" is a plain opposite. Line 1, "Love the LORD, all His saints", is a call with no part in the contrast, so the span is cut to lines 2 and 3.

places.why: "For they do not speak peace, but they devise deceitful schemes" describes the same people first by what they do not do and then by what they do. The two lines agree in sense, so they are not opposite lines, and no other form is plain.

The lines move from "the daughters of kings" to "the queen... at your right hand" and then to her gold. Each line adds and none restates the one before, and building is too loose to count as a plain figure.

"They are led in with joy and gladness; / they enter the palace of the king" completes the first line by saying where they go. That builds on it more than restating it, and the readers split, so when in doubt it does not go live.

places.why: "Your name, O God, like Your praise, / reaches to the ends of the earth" is one clause, and "Your right hand is full of righteousness" makes a new statement rather than restating it.

places.span_why: "I kept silent" is set against "But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face". "you thought I was just like you" adds a new thought.

places.why: "Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices... / then bulls will be offered on Your altar" moves from God's pleasure to the people's offering, so the second "then" adds rather than restates. The readers split, so when in doubt it does not go live.

"Will the workers of iniquity never learn? / They devour my people like bread; / they refuse to call upon God" adds a new charge in each line, first against the people and then against God. No line restates another.

Lines 1-2 ("Oh, that the salvation... / When God restores His captive people") restate nothing. The only pair, "let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!", sits inside one line of the BSB, so it cannot be marked as two lines. The tags also fall on words that have nothing to do with the pair.

"Hear my prayer, O God; / listen to the words of my mouth" plainly says one plea twice in the BSB itself. The only tag, H0238 "give ear", marks one verb of the pair and wrongly says the figure shows only in the original.

The figure is plain in the BSB. The only tag, H0238 on "give ear", marks half of the pair, and the figure does not show only in the original, so the tags are stripped.

places.why: "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! / I would fly away and find rest": the second line does not restate the wish. It says what would follow from it, so it plainly completes the first line. Kept as Built on, not Said twice.

"We shared sweet fellowship together; / we walked with the crowd into the house of God": the second line adds a new scene, worshipping together in public, to the private friendship of the first. That is plainly Built on, not a restatement.

"Let death seize them by surprise; / let them go down to Sheol alive" plainly says one curse twice. The third line, "for evil is with them in their homes", gives the reason and does not restate it, so only the first two lines are marked.

places.why: "All day long they twist my words; / all their thoughts are on my demise": both lines open with "all" and end on "my", so they are built alike, but the second line goes on from twisted words to plans for his death. "They conspire, they lurk, / they watch my steps / while they wait to take my life" is one sentence: a run of verbs that ends in a "while" clause. No line restates another, and the lines are not plainly a built pair either, so when in doubt it does not go live.

"In spite of such sin, will they escape?" is a question, and "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations" is a plea. The two lines are not built alike and the second does not restate the first, so neither same nor building plainly shows.

"He reaches down from heaven and saves me; / He rebukes those who trample me" are built alike ("He ... me"), and the second adds what He does to the foes. That is building, not same. "Selah" and the separate sentence "God sends forth / His loving devotion and His truth" are left out.

"Consume them in wrath; / consume them till they are no more": the second line takes up "consume them" and goes a step higher, so it is climbing. The purpose clause "so it may be known ... that God rules over Jacob" and "Selah" are left out.

"God has spoken once; / I have heard this twice" names a number and then the next one up, a numerical saying plain in the BSB's own words. It is not a restatement, and "that power belongs to God" is what was heard, so it is left out.

"They will fall to the power of the sword; / they will become a portion for foxes" is built alike ("they will ..."), and the second line tells what follows their death. It adds to the first, so it is building, not same.

places.why: "You divided the sea by Your strength; / You smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea": two lines built the same way ("You ...") that name two different deeds. The second adds rather than restates.
"You crushed the heads of Leviathan; / You fed him to the creatures of the desert": built the same way, and the second line tells what followed. It adds to the first rather than restating it.

"You broke open the fountain and the flood; / You dried up the ever-flowing rivers": opening springs and drying rivers are two different deeds, so this is not a restatement. Both lines are built the same way ("You ...") and each names a deed over the waters. That is plainly building. Calling them opposed in sense would be a stretch.

"You set all the boundaries of the earth; / You made the summer and winter": two lines built the same way that name two different works, one of the land and one of the seasons. The second adds rather than restates.

"We give thanks to You, O God; / we give thanks, for Your Name is near": the second line plainly says the first again. "The people declare Your wondrous works" brings in a new subject and act, so only the first two lines after the title are marked.

places.label_why: "We give thanks to You, O God; we give thanks, for Your Name is near." The second line takes up "we give thanks" and adds a reason, "for Your Name is near", so it builds on the first.

places.why: "I cried out to God; / I cried aloud to God to hear me" plainly says the cry twice. The only tag, H0238 ("and he will give ear"), is on the one element the second line adds. It is not on the repeated "my voice to God" that carries the parallel.

"Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind; / the lightning lit up the world; / the earth trembled and quaked": built the same way, and each line adds a step (thunder, lightning, the earth shaking) rather than restating the first.

places.why: "that they should put their confidence in God, / not forgetting His works, / but keeping His commandments": not forgetting His works and keeping His commandments agree, so no line sets an opposite. Each line adds one more duty, so the lines build.

The pair is plain in the BSB. The tags mark "and also" and leave out "fire" and "kindled", so they do not point at the figure.

places.why: Drove out the nations, apportioned the inheritance, settled the tribes: three acts in order, each line adding the next step. That is plainly built-on lines, not said twice. The span is the BSB's three lines.

"His priests fell by the sword, / but their widows could not lament" adds a second sorrow to the first. Nothing is set against it as an opposite. The second line plainly builds on the first, as in 78:63.

"He beat back His foes; / He put them to everlasting shame" is about the same enemies, but the second line adds a new outcome, lasting disgrace. Since it adds something rather than only restating, it is better marked as built on.

"His people Jacob" is said again as "Israel His inheritance", plainly in the BSB. "From tending the ewes He brought him" is not restated, so it comes out of the span. The tags leave out "inheritance", one of the paired words.

places.span_why: "How long, O LORD?" is the opening cry and calls on God. It does not restate the other lines. "Will You be angry forever?" is plainly said again in "Will Your jealousy burn like fire?"

"You uprooted a vine from Egypt; / You drove out the nations and transplanted it" goes on to the next steps, clearing the land and planting the vine. That is plainly built on, not a restatement.

"a statute for Israel, / an ordinance of the God of Jacob" pairs statute with ordinance and Israel with Jacob, plainly in the BSB. The tags mark "it" and leave out "statute", so they do not point at the figure.

"They do not know or understand; / they wander in the darkness" says their ignorance twice, the second time as walking in darkness. "All the foundations of the earth are shaken" is a new thought and comes out of the span.

places.why: The second line goes on with the complaint and adds God's terrors and his despair. There are no clear word pairs, so a restatement is not plain, but the second line plainly builds on the first. The span is the BSB's two lines.

places.label_why: "Will You hide Yourself forever? / Will Your wrath keep burning like fire?" The second question adds a different thing, God's burning wrath, to His hiding. It builds on the first rather than restating it.

So the second line adds a further point rather than restating the first.

places.why: "You have established equity; / You have exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob" plainly restate each other. Line 1, "The mighty King loves justice.", is about loving rather than doing, so it is doubtful as a restatement and is taken out.

places.why: "when will You come to me?" breaks in and restates nothing. "I will ponder the way that is blameless" and "I will walk in my house with integrity of heart" move from thinking to living, so the lines are not plainly said twice. No clear live form fits the marked lines.

places.label_why: The four lines run A B A' B': "No one who practices deceit / shall dwell in my house; / no one who tells lies / shall stand in my presence." Deceit matches lies and dwell matches stand, line for line, like the scarlet/snow pattern.

places.why: "I lie awake" is not said again by line 2, so this is not "said twice". The figure the verse plainly shows is the likeness with "like": "I am like a lone bird on a housetop." It is kept as a simile on that line.

Lines 2 to 4 continue the perishing and do not oppose line 1, so these are not opposite lines. The plain opposite sits inside line 1, "They will perish, but You remain", where perishing and remaining are set against each other. It is kept as antithesis on those words.

"As far as the east is from the west, / so far has He removed our transgressions from us" is one comparison. The second line completes the first and does not restate it, so these are lines that build, not said twice.

"As a father has compassion on his children, / so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him" is a plain "as... so" likeness between a father and the LORD. The second line is the thing compared, not a restatement, so it is kept as a simile on both lines.

"He wraps Himself in light as with a garment; / He stretches out the heavens like a tent" are built the same way, but the second line names a new act rather than restating the first. They are lines that build.

places.label: form
places.label_why: The four lines alternate: "When You give it to them, / they gather it up; / when You open Your hand, / they are satisfied with good things." Give pairs with open Your hand, and gather with satisfied, so they run A B A' B'.

places.why: "When You hide Your face, they are terrified; / when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust": the second pair is built like the first and goes a step further, from terror to death. It adds something and does not restate, so these are lines that build.

"May the glory of the LORD endure forever; / may the LORD rejoice in His works" are two wishes built the same way, and the second adds a different wish, the LORD's joy in His works. They are lines that build, not said twice.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "He looks on the earth, / and it trembles; / He touches the mountains, / and they smolder" runs A B A' B': looks on the earth/touches the mountains, trembles/smolder.

places.why: "Sing to Him, sing praises to Him; / tell of all His wonders": the second line adds a new act, telling His wonders, to the call to sing. The repeated "sing" is inside line 1 and is not a restatement between the lines, so these are lines that build.

"He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree, / to Israel as an everlasting covenant" plainly says the same thing twice: Jacob is Israel, and the decree is the covenant. This shows in the BSB itself, so the claim that it shows only in the original is wrong. The tags mark decree but not covenant (H1285), so they cover only half the pairs. They are dropped.

places.label_why: "He let no man oppress them; He rebuked kings on their behalf": the second line adds another act. He did more than keep them from harm, He rebuked kings, so it builds on the first line and does not restate it.

places.why: "Then Israel entered Egypt; / Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham" plainly restates itself: Israel is Jacob and Egypt is the land of Ham. It shows in the BSB, not only in the Hebrew. The tags mark Egypt but not Ham (H2526H), so they cover only half the pairs. They are dropped.

places.why: "did not grasp Your wonders / or remember Your abundant kindness; / but they rebelled by the sea" sets up no opposite. The "but" adds a worse sin by the same people. The four lines mix restatement and addition, and no single relation is plain enough to go live unsourced.

"He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up; / He led them through the depths as through a desert" tells two steps in order. The second line is a new act, not a restatement. The two lines are not built in a strikingly similar way either, so calling them building would be only a loose claim.

"They despised the pleasant land" and "they did not believe His promise" name two different failings, and the second gives the root unbelief. The words are not synonyms, so a reader would need help to call this "said twice". It is doubtful, so it fails.

places.span_why: The opposite is "Many times He rescued them" against "but they were bent on rebellion". The line "and sank down in their iniquity" continues the second line and does not oppose it.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "He blesses them, and they multiply greatly; He does not let their herds diminish": the second line adds something new, their herds as well as the people themselves, so it builds on the first line.

places.why: "I will parcel out Shechem / and apportion the Valley of Succoth" plainly says the same act twice in other words: "parcel out" and "apportion" mean the same, each said of a portion of the land. "God has spoken from His sanctuary:" only introduces the speech, and "I will triumph!" is not restated. Only lines 3 and 4 are marked.

places.why: In "May his days be few; / may another take his position", the second line adds a new curse, the loss of his office. It does not restate the first. Calling it building would be a loose claim with nothing striking in the words.
In "he never thought to show kindness, / but pursued the poor and needy", both lines condemn the same man, and the "but" goes further. The lines agree in sense, so they are not opposite lines.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "The cursing that he loved, / may it fall on him; / the blessing in which he refused to delight, / may it be far from him" runs A B A' B': cursing loved/blessing refused, fall on him/be far from him.

places.why: "When they rise up, they will be put to shame, / but Your servant will rejoice" plainly sets the opposite against the line before. Line 1 ("Though they curse, You will bless.") holds its own contrast inside one BSB line and does not stand opposite line 2. Only lines 2 and 3 are marked.

"He provides food for those who fear Him; / He remembers His covenant forever" makes two different statements. The second does not restate the first, and calling it building would be only a loose claim.

"He has sent redemption to His people; / He has ordained His covenant forever; / holy and awesome is His name" makes three different statements, and the third is praise of His name. No line restates another.
"He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; / his righteousness endures forever; / his horn will be lifted high in honor" adds something new in each line. None restates another.

"Not to us, O LORD, not to us, / but to Your name be the glory" plainly sets the opposite against the first line: not us, but Your name. Lines 3 and 4 ("because of Your loving devotion, / because of Your faithfulness") give the reason and are not part of the contrast, so only lines 1 and 2 are marked.

"They have mouths, but cannot speak; / they have eyes, but cannot see" has its "but" inside each line, so the lines are not opposite. Both lines are plainly built the same way (they have X, but cannot Y), and the second adds another organ to the first. That is building.

"they have ears, but cannot hear; / they have noses, but cannot smell" has its contrast inside each line, so the lines are not opposite. Both lines are plainly built the same way, and the second adds another organ. That is building.

"they have hands, but cannot feel; / they have feet, but cannot walk; / they cannot even clear their throats" has its "but" inside each line, so no line opposes another. The first two lines are built the same way, and the third adds the last organ and completes the list. That is building.

"Those who make them become like them, / as do all who trust in them" is one sentence that "as do" extends to a second group. It is not a restatement, and calling it building would be only a loose claim.

The lines are not restatements: each names a different group. They plainly begin alike, "He will bless" three times in a row (and again in 115:13), so they are kept as Like beginnings. "The LORD is mindful of us;" does not share the pattern and is left out.

"They surrounded me on every side, / but in the name of the LORD I cut them off" tells of a threat and then a rescue. The second line does not set the opposite of the first against it, so no live form is plain at these lines.

Swarming and being put out are an attack and its end, not opposite lines, and the mark also took in the refrain line. The plain figures are the two likenesses with "like": "like bees" and "like burning thorns".
"I was pushed so hard I was falling, / but the LORD helped me" moves from danger to rescue. "Helped" is not the stated opposite of "falling", so opposite lines are not plain.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "The right hand of the LORD is exalted! / The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!" Only the subject repeats. "Performs with valor" adds a second praise and does not put "is exalted" another way, so the second line builds on the first.

places.why: Line 2, "and proclaim what the LORD has done", adds to line 1 and does not oppose it, so the two lines are not opposite lines. But line 1 plainly sets opposites together: "I will not die, but I will live".
"The LORD disciplined me severely, / but He has not given me over to death" puts a limit on the discipline. Discipline and death are not set as opposites, so opposite lines are not plain.

"and I will not be ashamed" adds something new and does not say the first line again. The lines are at most "built on" in the loose sense true of almost any two lines, which is not a plain figure, so the place does not go live.

"The arrogant utterly deride me, / but I do not turn from Your law" means "despite their scorn, I hold fast". Not turning from the law is not the opposite of deriding, so opposite lines are not plain.
"teach me Your statutes" is a request that follows from the praise in line 1. It does not restate it, and a loose "built on" link is not a plain figure.
"They almost wiped me from the earth, / but I have not forsaken Your precepts" means "faithful in spite of attack". The second line does not state the opposite of the first.
"The wicked wait to destroy me, / but I will ponder Your testimonies": pondering is not the opposite of lying in wait. The "but" marks a response, not opposite lines.
"The wicked have set a snare for me, / but I have not strayed from Your precepts" means "despite the trap, I did not stray". No opposites are set against each other.
"I am lowly and despised, / but I do not forget Your precepts" means "faithful though despised". Not forgetting is not the opposite of being lowly.
"Rulers persecute me without cause, / but my heart fears only Your word" means "though persecuted". Any contrast between what is feared is only implied, so opposite lines are not plain.

"What will He do to you, / and what will be added to you" plainly asks the same question twice in other words. Line 3, "O deceitful tongue?", addresses the tongue and restates nothing, so the mark is cut to lines 1 and 2.

"May the LORD bless you from Zion, / that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem": the second line gives the purpose of the blessing and does not restate the first, in the BSB or in the Hebrew. The tags on "and look" and "good things" carry no figure.

"many a time they have persecuted me from my youth, / but they have not prevailed against me" means "attacked, yet not beaten". Not prevailing is not the opposite of persecuting, so opposite lines are not plain.
The three lines do not say one thing twice: line 3 takes up line 2 and completes it. The plain figure is the likeness with "like": "like a weaned child is my soul within me".

"We heard that the ark was in Ephrathah; / we found it in the fields of Jaar" moves the story from hearing to finding. It does not say the first line again, and a loose "built on" link is not a plain figure.

The tags fall on "chosen" and "Yah" and miss "possession", so they do not point at the figure.

places.why: "they have ears, but cannot hear; / nor is there breath in their mouths": the second line adds a further lack and does not oppose the first. A loose "built on" link is not a plain figure. The one tag, "they give ear", carries nothing between the lines.

"As do all who trust in them" does not say the first line again; it carries the same fate ("become like them") on from the makers to everyone who trusts in idols. places.label_why: "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD." Each line calls a further group, and v20 adds Levi and those who fear the LORD. It is a list, not a restatement.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "Blessed be the LORD from Zion— He who dwells in Jerusalem." The second line does not repeat the blessing. It completes the first by describing the LORD as the One who dwells in Jerusalem.

places.label_why: "You know when I sit and when I rise; You understand my thoughts from afar." The second line adds something new: God knows not only my outward movements but my inner thoughts.

places.why: All four lines are marked as one restatement, but "It is oil for my head" adds a picture and "For my prayer is ever against the deeds of the wicked" is a new thought. Even line 2 adds a judgment ("an act of loving devotion") to "strike me" instead of restating it. No live parallel form fits these lines plainly.

"As when one plows and breaks up the soil, / so our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol." is an open As ... so likeness. The second line is the thing being compared, not a restatement. The figure is plain, so the place stays under simile with both lines, which hold both sides of the likeness.

places.span_why: "O LORD, hear my prayer" and "In Your faithfulness, give ear to my plea" plainly make the same request. "in Your righteousness, answer me" asks for more than being heard, so only the first two lines are kept. The one tag, on "give ear", marks one word of one line and not the parallel itself.
places.label: all

places.why: "supplying all manner of produce" completes "Our storehouses will be full". The flocks lines bring a different blessing and raise thousands to tens of thousands. No line says the one before it again, and the four lines do not plainly stand in any single live relation.

The second line gives a new and deeper ground ("whose God is the LORD"), so it is not a plain restatement. What the words plainly show is that both lines open with "Blessed are the people", which is Like beginnings. So the place stays under that form, marked on the repeated words.

"Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, / and Your dominion endures through all generations." is a plain restatement. "The LORD is faithful in all His words / and kind in all His actions" is a separate couplet that does not restate the kingdom lines. So the marked words narrow to the first pair.

places.label_why: "He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; / He hears their cry and saves them": the second line adds more acts, hearing their cry and saving them. It does not say the first again in matching words.

places.why: "How good it is to sing praises to our God, / how pleasant and lovely to praise Him!" is a plain restatement. The separate line "Hallelujah!" is no part of it, so it comes off the marked words.

places.label_why: "He determines the number of the stars; / He calls them each by name": counting the stars and naming each one are two different acts. The second line goes past the total to each star.

places.why: "He makes peace at your borders; / He fills you with the finest wheat." names two different gifts, peace and food. The second line does not restate the first, and calling one gift added to another "Built on" is too loose to show plainly.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "He spreads the snow like wool; / He scatters the frost like ashes": the second line names a different thing, frost, with its own likeness, and adds it to the snow. The next verse goes on to hail.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "He sends forth His word and melts them; / He unleashes His winds, and the waters flow": the second line adds another thing God sends, His winds, and a further result, the waters flowing.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "Praise Him, O sun and moon; / praise Him, all you shining stars": the second line calls on different lights, the stars, and adds them to the sun and moon. It does not say the first again.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "Praise Him with the sound of the horn; / praise Him with the harp and lyre": the second line adds different instruments to the horn. It does not say the first again in other words.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; / praise Him with strings and flute": the second line adds different instruments to the first. It does not restate it.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "We will find all manner of precious goods; / we will fill our houses with plunder": the second line goes a step past finding the goods, to filling their houses with them.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "How long, O simple ones, will you love your simple ways? / How long will scoffers delight in their scorn / and fools hate knowledge?": each line adds a different group with its own failing, so the lines build on one another.

places.why: "Then they will call on me, but I will not answer; they will earnestly seek me, but will not find me": each "but" falls inside its own line. The second line restates the first (call/seek, not answer/not find), so the lines are "same", not "opposite". The marked words are the BSB's two lines.

places.why: "He stores up sound wisdom for the upright; He is a shield to those who walk with integrity": the two lines plainly match (He ... for the upright / He ... to those who walk with integrity). But the second line adds a new gift, protection, and does not restate the stored-up wisdom. So it is building, not "same".

"My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments": the second line gives the same charge in positive form (keep my commandments = do not forget my teaching). Despite the "but", it sets no opposite against the first line, so this is "same".
places.label: all

places.why: "Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn from them": the second line does not say "get wisdom" again. It adds a matching charge to hold fast to the father's words (as in 4:4), so it builds on the first line rather than restating it.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "She does not consider the path of life" is followed by a new fact, "she does not know that her ways are unstable"; the second line adds that her ways wander, it does not restate the first.

places.why: "May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth": the two wishes are plainly parallel, and after 5:15-17 the second line says outright who "your fountain" is. It also adds the husband's delight in her, so it does more than restate the first line. Building fits plainly; "same" is doubtful.

"When you walk, they will guide you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; when you awake, they will speak to you": three plainly matching lines. Each one adds a new time and a new help (guide, watch over, speak), so the lines build on one another rather than say the first again.

"I saw among the simple, I noticed among the youths" plainly says the same thing twice (saw/noticed, simple/youths). The third line, "a young man lacking judgment," is the object of both verbs and restates neither, so only the first two lines are marked.
places.label: all

places.why: "Now in the street, now in the squares, she lurks at every corner": the first line has no verb, and the second completes it ("she lurks"). Since the second line completes the first rather than restating it, this is building.

"She seizes him and kisses him; she brazenly says to him:": this is plain narrative sequence, and the second line only opens her speech in 7:14. It does not restate the first line, and calling it a built-on parallel would be a stretch, so it is not plain enough to go live.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "So I came out to meet you; / I sought you, and I have found you." "Sought" takes up "came out to meet", but the line goes on to the result, "and I have found you". It adds the outcome, so it builds on the first line rather than only saying it again.

places.why: "when He established the clouds above, / when the fountains of the deep gushed forth": the two BSB poetry lines run in parallel ("when ... when"), but the second names a different work, the deep below after the clouds above. It adds to the first line and does not say it again, so this is Built on, not Said twice. The marked words are the BSB's own two lines.

"She has prepared her meat and mixed her wine; / she has also set her table.": the word "also" plainly marks a further step in the feast, a new act and not a restatement. This is Built on. The marked words are the BSB's own two lines.

"She has sent out her maidservants; / she calls out from the heights of the city.": the second line adds a new act (her own call, and where it is made) to the sending. It does not restate it, so this is Built on. The marked words are the BSB's own two lines.

"Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, / so is the slacker to those who send him.": the second line does not restate the first. It names what the likeness is about, so the figure is a simile and not Said twice. No parallel-lines form fits cleanly. The simile at this verse is already its own place (proverbs-10-26-simile-seen, words-14 #347, marked "Like vinegar"), so moving this one to simile would make a second copy. Drop it.

The BSB sets two lines: "Abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, / but without justice it is swept away." The second line goes on about the same food ("it") and tells what becomes of it, so it completes the first line. It does not set an opposite subject against the first, so "opposite" is not plain, but "building" is. The marked words are the BSB's own two lines, and the place has no Strong's tags.

The BSB sets two lines: "There is a way that seems right to a man, / but its end is the way of death." The second line takes up the same way ("its end") and finishes the thought by telling where it leads. That is a line that completes the first, not a line that sets an opposite against it, so the right form is "building". The marked words are the BSB's own two lines, and the place has no Strong's tags.

The two lines are plainly parallel ("By loving devotion and faithfulness...; and by the fear of the LORD..."). But "iniquity is atoned for" and "one turns aside from evil" are different things, so the second line adds a further means and result rather than saying the first again. "Built on" fits; "Said twice" is not plain.

"but a wise man will pacify it" points back to the same wrath ("it") and tells what a wise man does with it. That completes the first line. There is no clean opposite term set against "messenger of death", so "Opposite lines" can be argued but is not plain. "Built on" is plainly true.

"A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold" has no verb and is completed by "but the LORD is the tester of hearts". The lines draw a likeness (as fire tests metal, the LORD tests hearts), not an opposite. The second line completes the first, so the form is "Built on".

"A wicked man listens to evil lips; a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue" plainly says the same thing twice: wicked man and liar, listens and gives ear, evil lips and destructive tongue. The figure is in both whole lines. The single tag H0238 ("giving ear") marks one half of one paired verb, with its partner H7181 left untagged, so it does not point at what carries the figure.
places.label: all

places.why: "He who loves transgression loves strife; he who builds his gate high invites destruction" is plainly parallel ("He who...; he who..."). The second line is a new picture with a new outcome, though, and a reader would only take it as a restatement if a commentary told him the high gate means pride. It adds a second case, so "Built on" fits and "Said twice" does not.

"He who isolates himself pursues selfish desires; he rebels against all sound judgment" keeps the same man as subject and adds a further charge against him. The second line goes on from the first rather than plainly saying it again, so the form is "Built on".

"A fool does not delight in understanding, but only in airing his opinions" is one sentence about one fool. The second line cannot stand alone and finishes the first ("not ... but only"). There is a contrast inside the sentence, but it is not a second line set against the first as its opposite. "Built on" (it completes the first line) is the form that is plainly right.

"The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe": the second line takes the tower picture further (running to it, being safe). It does not restate the first line, so the form is "Built on".

No line here sets an opposite against the first. Each of the four BSB lines adds to the one before: the brothers hate him, "how much more" the friends avoid him, he pleads with them, and they are nowhere to be found. Marking the whole group of four lines as "Built on" is plain and uses the BSB's own lines.

"The slacker does not plow in season; at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there": the second line gives the result of the first. The only "but" falls inside line 2, so the lines are cause and consequence, not opposites. The form is "Built on".

"When a mocker is punished, the simple gain wisdom; and when a wise man is instructed, he acquires knowledge" is plainly parallel in shape. The second line sets a second case beside the first, with a different learner who learns in a different way, so it adds rather than restates. The form is "Built on".

"Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, / but the rod of discipline drives it far from him." The second line gives the cure for what the first line describes. It does not state the opposite truth, so the lines are plainly Built on, not Opposite lines.

Only lines 2 and 3 say the same thing twice: "He will be stationed in the presence of kings; / he will not stand before obscure men." Line 1 is the question they answer, so the place is cut to those two lines.
places.label: all

places.why: Lines 3 and 4 plainly set his welcoming words against his heart: "'Eat and drink,' he says to you, / but his heart is not with you." Lines 1 and 2 restate each other and are not part of that contrast, so the place is cut to lines 3 and 4.

Each line names different troubles, so no line restates another. All six questions plainly open with the same words, "Who has", which is Like beginnings. The whole verse is made of those clauses, so the three lines stay marked.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "Your eyes will see strange things" is followed by another effect, "your mind will utter perversities"; seeing and speaking are two acts, so the second line adds to the first.

places.why: The "but" falls inside each line, not between lines. "They struck me, but I feel no pain! / They beat me, but I did not know it!" says the same thing twice (struck/beat, no pain/did not know). Lines 3 and 4 are one question and stand in neither relation.

places.label_why: "Do not lie in wait ... near the dwelling of the righteous" is followed by a further act, "do not destroy his resting place"; lying in wait and destroying are two acts, so the second line goes on from the first.

places.why: "As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, / so the hearts of kings cannot be searched" is a plain likeness built on "as ... so". The second line applies the picture to kings and does not restate it.
"As the north wind brings forth rain, / so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks" is a plain "as ... so" likeness between weather and the tongue, not a restatement.
"As a dog returns to its vomit, / so a fool repeats his folly" is a plain "as ... so" likeness, not one line saying the other again.
"As a door turns on its hinges, / so the slacker turns on his bed" is a plain "as ... so" likeness, not a restatement.

"Without wood, a fire goes out; / without gossip, a conflict ceases" sets a picture beside its lesson, with no "like" or "as". The second line applies the first and does not restate it. No live form fits exactly, and the matching "without" is English only (the Hebrew uses two different words), so it stays out.
"Like charcoal for embers and wood for fire, / so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife" is a plain "like ... so" likeness, not a restatement.

"A hateful man disguises himself with his speech, / but he lays up deceit in his heart." Line 1 already says the speech is a disguise, so line 2 does not oppose it. It completes it by saying what the disguise hides, which is plainly Built on.

"A stone is heavy and sand is a burden, / but aggravation from a fool outweighs them both." The second line goes beyond the first ("outweighs them both") and does not set its opposite, so it is plainly Built on.

"Wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, / but who can withstand jealousy?" The second line goes a step past the first: jealousy is worse still. It does not state the first line's opposite, so it is plainly Built on.
"As iron sharpens iron, / so one man sharpens another" is a plain "as ... so" likeness, not a restatement.
"As water reflects the face, / so the heart reflects the true man" is a plain "as ... so" likeness, not a restatement.

"A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, / but a man is tested by the praise accorded him" sets metal tested by fire beside a man tested by praise. That is a likeness with no "like" or "as", not an opposite, and no live form fits it exactly, so it stays out.

"he receives the oath, but does not testify" does not set an opposite against "A partner to a thief hates his own soul". The "but" sits inside line 2. How line 2 completes line 1 depends on knowing the law of the oath, so even "building" is not plain from the BSB alone. When in doubt, drop. The verse is also marked as a proverb elsewhere (proverbs-29-24-proverb-seen).

Each line names a different act, so no line restates another and "said twice" is wrong. The plain figure is a run of questions that are not asking, which the challenge "surely you know!" makes clear. Marked on the five question lines; "surely you know!" is not a question. Note: this overlaps proverbs-30-4-question-seen (words-06 #678), which marks only line 1, so the two should be merged.

"What shall I say, O my son? / What, O son of my womb? / What, O son of my vows?" Each line repeats "What, O son" and adds something, first "of my womb" and then "of my vows", so the address grows stronger line by line. That fits Climbing lines better than a plain restatement. Since "Said twice" is in doubt here, the place fails.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchants." The second line names a second thing she supplies (sashes) and who buys them (the merchants), so it adds to the first rather than saying it again.

places.label: form
places.label_why: "Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband praises her as well." The words "as well" show the second line adding another person who praises her.

places.why: "but you surpass them all!" does not contradict "Many daughters have done noble things". It goes beyond it, so the second line plainly completes and builds on the first. Kept as "building" on the same two BSB lines.

"for you do not know what disaster may befall the land" is the reason for the command "Divide your portion among seven, or even eight". It does not restate it, and a command with its reason is ordinary syntax, not a plain pair of parallel lines. The real figure, "seven, or even eight", is already a cited numbers place (handoff-24 #160, two writers), so moving this one to "numbers" would duplicate it.

Only lines 3 and 4 say the same thing twice: "We will rejoice and delight in you; / we will praise your love more than wine." "Take me away with you", "May the king bring me to his chambers" and "It is only right that they adore you" restate neither line, so the marked words are cut to those two lines.

places.label_why: "Your cheeks are beautiful with ornaments, / your neck with strings of jewels." The second line has no verb of its own. It completes the first by adding a second adorned part, the neck, so it builds on it.

places.why: "His left hand is under my head, / and his right arm embraces me." The second line names the other arm doing a different act, so it does not restate the first. It plainly completes the one picture of the embrace, so it is kept as "building" on the same two lines. The refrain place on these lines (words-10 #613) is a different form and does not conflict.

Three clauses are built the same way, and each adds a new sign of spring: "The flowers have appeared", "the season of singing has come", "the cooing of turtledoves / is heard". None restates another, and lines 3 and 4 are one clause, so "said twice" is wrong. The four lines are marked as a whole group under "building".

"Arise, come away, my darling; / come away with me, my beautiful one" plainly says one call twice in other words. The fig tree and vines lines are a different thought and do not restate the call, so the marked words are cut to lines 3 and 4.
places.label: all

places.why: "On my bed at night" is only the setting, and "but did not find him" tells how the search ended. No line sets an opposite against another. The repeated "I sought" is not plain enough to call climbing lines without a commentary, so the place is dropped.

The brow lines praise a different feature and restate neither earlier line. Whether "and your mouth is lovely" restates "Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon" is uncertain (both readers hedged), so "said twice" does not go live. The plain figure is the likeness "Your brow ... is like a slice of pomegranate". Only that simile is marked, because "like a scarlet" is already marked by song-of-solomon-4-3-simile-seen (words-14 #428).

places.span_why: "You have captured my heart" and "you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes" say the same thing. "my sister, my bride" only addresses her, and "with one jewel of your neck" finishes the second clause.
places.label: all

places.why: "Eat, O friends, and drink; / drink freely, O beloved" plainly says the call twice, with "friends" matched by "beloved". The first four lines, from "I have come to my garden" on, are a different thought (what he has done) and are not restated by the call, so six lines as one restatement is wrong. The marked words are cut to lines 5 and 6.

places.why: No two lines are set against each other; "I sleep, but my heart is awake" is a contrast inside one line. The plain pair is lines 5-6, "My head is drenched with dew, / my hair with the dampness of the night" (head/hair, dew/dampness of the night), which says the same thing twice. Kept as said twice on those two lines only.
